note: Starter Daily Dharma rotation. Plain text only. Each entry: teaching + plain meaning + one practical try + one reply hint. Reviewed content; the LLM does not rewrite these.

entries.message:
TODAY'S DHARMA

“You have a right to action, but not to its results.” — Bhagavad Gita 2.47

This does not mean results don't matter. It means your peace should not depend entirely on controlling an outcome that was never fully yours to control.

Try today: Before one stressful task, ask, “What part of this is actually under my control?”

Want the deeper meaning or the sources? Just ask.

TODAY'S DHARMA

“Let a person lift themselves by their own self; let them not degrade themselves.” — Bhagavad Gita 6.5

The mind can be your closest friend or your hardest opponent. Hindu teaching on discipline begins here: you are not asked to be perfect, only to take your own side patiently.

Try today: Notice one self-critical thought and answer it the way you would answer a friend.

Want the deeper meaning or the sources? Just ask.

TODAY'S DHARMA

The Isha Upanishad opens: “All this, whatever moves in this moving world, is pervaded by the Divine.” (Isha 1)

If the sacred pervades everything, then ordinary things — your desk, your commute, the person in front of you — are not interruptions to spiritual life. They are where it happens.

Try today: Treat one routine task as if it mattered. Do it with full attention.

Want the deeper meaning or the sources? Just ask.

TODAY'S DHARMA

Seva — selfless service — is one of Hinduism's most widely shared practices. Serving others without expecting recognition is treated across traditions as a direct spiritual discipline, not a side activity.

A small act done sincerely counts. The tradition does not require grand gestures.

Try today: Do one helpful thing quietly, without mentioning it to anyone.

Want the deeper meaning or a practice to try? Just ask.

TODAY'S DHARMA

Santosha — contentment — appears in the Yoga Sutras (2.42) among the personal disciplines. It is not passivity; it is refusing to postpone your peace until conditions are perfect.

You can work to change things and be at peace while you do. The tradition treats those as compatible, not opposites.

Try today: Name three things that are already enough, exactly as they are.

Want the deeper meaning or the sources? Just ask.

TODAY'S DHARMA

“Contacts of the senses with their objects give rise to cold and heat, pleasure and pain. They come and go; they are impermanent. Endure them.” — Bhagavad Gita 2.14

Difficult feelings are real, but they are weather, not climate. Hindu teaching often begins not by fixing emotion but by watching it move.

Try today: When irritation rises, silently note “this will pass” — and watch whether it does.

Want the deeper meaning or the sources? Just ask.

TODAY'S DHARMA

Ahimsa — non-harm — is listed first among the restraints in the Yoga Sutras (2.35) and honored across Hindu traditions. It covers more than physical harm: speech and even inner attitude count.

Most of us will not strike anyone today. But sarcasm, contempt, and harsh self-talk are also within ahimsa's reach.

Try today: Soften one sentence you were about to say sharply.

Want the deeper meaning or the sources? Just ask.

TODAY'S DHARMA

The Gita (3.12–13) describes life as sustained by a cycle of giving — the idea behind yajna, offering. What we receive, we receive from a web of others: farmers, parents, teachers, strangers.

Gratitude in Hindu practice is not a mood. It is an accurate reading of how much arrives in your hands unearned.

Try today: Before one meal, pause and silently name where the food came from.

Want the deeper meaning or the sources? Just ask.

TODAY'S DHARMA

In the Katha Upanishad, a boy named Nachiketa refuses comfortable answers about death and keeps asking until Yama, Death himself, teaches him. The tradition preserves his story as praise for honest questioning.

Doubt handled honestly is not the opposite of faith here — it is one of its forms.

Try today: Ask one question you've been embarrassed not to know the answer to.

Want the full story or the sources? Just ask.

TODAY'S DHARMA

The Gita (17.15) describes the discipline of speech: words that are truthful, kind, and helpful. All three together — truth without kindness and kindness without truth both fall short.

Try today: Before one difficult message or reply, check it against all three: is it true, is it kind, does it help?

Want the deeper meaning or the sources? Just ask.

TODAY'S DHARMA

Many Hindu prayers end “Om shanti shanti shanti” — peace repeated three times, traditionally for the body, the world around us, and forces beyond our control.

The repetition is honest: peace has to be made in more than one place, more than once.

Try today: Take three slow breaths, one for each shanti, before you open your messages in the morning.

Want the deeper meaning or a practice to try? Just ask.

TODAY'S DHARMA

Dharma is context-sensitive: the Mahabharata repeatedly shows that the right act depends on your role, your moment, and who depends on you. A parent's duty, a student's duty, and a leader's duty differ — and can pull against each other.

Hindu ethics takes that tension seriously instead of pretending one rule fits all.

Try today: Name the two duties currently pulling at you. Just naming them is the first step.

Want the deeper meaning or the sources? Just ask.
